summary: Describes a mechanism for signaling that compression is wanted for SIP messages, and states when it is appropriate to send compressed SIP messages to another SIP entity. It builds on the Signaling Compression framework.

eli5.summary: SIP messages are chatty. This note lets two devices agree to squeeze their messages smaller, and tells them when that is safe to do.

questions: why not use dns to signal sip compression
subtitle: How SIP endpoints signal, with a simple URI and Via parameter, that they accept SigComp-compressed messages.

tldr.problem: SIP could advertise optional layers such as TLS or compression through DNS, but every combination of transport, security and compression would need its own DNS entry. A server with two transports, TLS and SigComp would need 8.
tldr.mechanism: A comp=sigcomp parameter on a SIP URI or on a Via header says the entity supports SigComp and is willing to receive compressed messages. Clients and servers then compress requests and responses only when they have seen it.
tldr.outcome: Compression is negotiated at the SIP layer with no extra DNS records. A compressed request to a server that does not understand SigComp cannot be answered, so clients retry uncompressed after a timeout. RFC 5049 later updated this RFC.

facts.label: Token length
facts.value: SHOULD be no more than ten characters

today: RFC 3486 is a Proposed Standard that has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 5049, so read the two together.

sections.title: Why Not Use DNS
sections.content:
A SIP client usually does a DNS lookup for the server's domain. With NAPTR or SRV records it can pick a service, which here means the transport: UDP, TCP or SCTP. One entry per transport is manageable.

Extra layers between transport and application, such as transport security and compression, break that. A server supporting TCP and SCTP, with TLS and SigComp, would need 8 DNS entries, one for each combination. The RFC concludes this is not scalable and that an application layer mechanism to express support for signaling compression is needed.

A SIP element that supports compression must be ready to receive compressed and uncompressed messages on the same port, telling them apart by the cookie in the topmost bits of each compressed message.
sections.eli5: Writing a separate phone book entry for every way to reach someone would make a huge book. It is easier to ask them directly how they like to be reached.

sections.title: The comp Parameter
sections.content:
The RFC defines one parameter in two places: a SIP URI parameter and a Via header parameter. Both look the same, for example sip:alice@atlanta.com;comp=sigcomp and a Via header ending in ;comp=sigcomp.

In a URI, comp=sigcomp means requests to it have to be compressed using SigComp. In a Via header, it means the response has to be compressed. Together this signals both that the entity supports SigComp and that it is willing to receive compressed messages. Meaning 'willing' as well as 'supports' lets the receiver influence whether compression is used at a given time. Every SIP implementation that supports SigComp MUST implement these procedures.
sections.eli5: The tag on an address says 'send me shrunk messages'. If it is not there, send normal ones.

sections.title: Sending Requests and Responses
sections.content:
A request goes to the next-hop URI, which is the Request-URI or an entry in the Route header. If that URI has comp=sigcomp, the client SHOULD compress the request. For a SIPS URI, the request is compressed before it goes to the TLS layer. A client MUST NOT send a compressed request if it does not know whether the server supports SigComp.

A client that wants later requests in the dialog compressed in the opposite direction adds comp=sigcomp to its Contact URI (a user agent) or its Record-Route URI (a proxy). A client that sends a compressed request SHOULD add the parameter to the topmost Via. A client that is unsure about support but would welcome compressed responses also adds it to the topmost Via, although its request goes out uncompressed.

For responses, if the topmost Via has comp=sigcomp, the response SHOULD be compressed. Otherwise it MUST NOT be compressed.
sections.eli5: Only shrink a message for someone who has said they can unshrink it. Replies follow the same tag on the original request.

sections.title: Finding Compressed URIs and Avoiding One-Way Compression
sections.content:
Within a dialog, a comp=sigcomp next-hop URI comes from the Record-Route header. Outside a dialog, clients may find one in a Contact header of a 3xx or 485 response. Since users should not have to wait for a dialog before compressing the initial INVITE, a client can send an uncompressed OPTIONS request to its outbound proxy. The proxy may answer with a 200 OK whose Contact header lists an alternative URI with comp=sigcomp. The RFC extends the RFC 3261 behavior for 200 responses to OPTIONS addressed to a proxy. User agents can also REGISTER a URI with comp=sigcomp, so incoming requests reach them compressed.

To avoid asymmetric compression, where one direction is compressed and the other is not, a proxy that Record-Routes inspects the Record-Route in the response and the Contact in the triggering request. If the next upstream hop URI has comp=sigcomp, the proxy SHOULD add it to its own Record-Route entry, otherwise it SHOULD remove it. A user agent server likewise adds it to its Contact in the response.

Some proxies, such as a firewall between two networks, add two Record-Route entries to avoid this rewriting. A proxy MAY also skip compression when the next hop is itself.
sections.eli5: Proxies make sure both sides agree. If one side talks in shorthand, the middleman tells the other side it can too, so neither talks past the other.

sections.title: Error Situations
sections.content:
If a compressed request reaches a server that does not understand SigComp, the server cannot even parse it, and there is no Via header to say where to send an error. The client therefore has to cope.

If a client sends a compressed request and the transaction times out with no response, the client SHOULD retry the same request without compression. If the compressed request went over TCP, the client SHOULD close that connection and open a new one for the uncompressed request, because otherwise the server could not detect the beginning of the new message.
sections.eli5: If you speak shorthand and get no answer, try again in plain words, on a fresh phone call.

sections.title: Call Flow Example
sections.content:
The RFC walks through an INVITE, 200 OK and ACK between a UAC and a UAS via proxies P1 and P2. Both proxies support compression but do not use it by default. P1 does not Record-Route and P2 does.

The UAC is configured to send compressed traffic to P1, so it compresses the INVITE and puts comp=sigcomp in Via and Contact. P1 and P2 forward the INVITE uncompressed. When P2 sees the 200 OK, it notes that the UAC's Contact wants compression and adds comp=sigcomp to its Record-Route entry. P1 sends the 200 OK compressed to the UAC because of the Via parameter. The UAC then sends the ACK compressed straight to P2, and P2 forwards it uncompressed to the UAS.
sections.eli5: Only the legs of the trip where both sides said 'shorthand is fine' use shorthand. The other legs stay in plain words.

sections.title: Security and Registry
sections.content:
A receiver must decompress and then parse a compressed message, which takes slightly more processing than parsing alone. A denial of service attack using compressed messages would therefore be slightly worse than one using uncompressed messages.

An attacker who inserts comp=sigcomp into a SIP message could make one entity send compressed messages to another that does not support SigComp, so appropriate integrity mechanisms should be used.

The RFC defines the comp URI parameter and Via extension and lets IANA register new values when new signaling compression schemes appear in standards track RFCs. A token MAY be any length but SHOULD be no more than ten characters. The only entry is sigcomp for Signaling Compression.
sections.eli5: Someone could fake the tag and trick a device into sending shorthand to a friend who cannot read it, so the tag should be protected from tampering.
